title: Distinguishing Coherent Crosstalk from Calibration Drift via Pauli-Transfer Signatures and Quantum Edge Detection
authors: Syed Emad Uddin Shubha, Tasnuva Farheen
abstract: Multi-tenant quantum processors expose a pulse-level attack surface in which coherent crosstalk can mimic benign calibration drift at matched average gate infidelity. We present a structural verification and detection framework based on the residual Pauli transfer matrix (PTM). We prove that products of local unital, trace-preserving channels cannot mix weight-1 and weight-2 Pauli operators, even under coherent drift of arbitrary strength or axis. Building on established PTM-to-Hamiltonian relations, we prove that, for any specified qubit pair in an arbitrarily large system, the first-order map from its nine interaction coefficients to the antisymmetric cross-weight feature is an isometry up to scale. Thus, every interaction direction is locally observable near the identity. We also exhibit cancellation of this feature under large local rotations and prove that the full cross-weight norm is invariant under local unitary composition, providing a structural countermeasure. For calibrated small local rotations, shared randomized-Pauli measurements support periodic verification using the evaluated antisymmetric detector. In simulation, $16{,}384$ randomized settings yield a detection threshold of $λ_{\min}\approx0.13$ at a $5\%$ calibrated false-positive target, with approximately $M^{-1/2}$ scaling in the number of settings $M$. Further experiments characterize detection under relaxation, depolarization, native ZZ fluctuations, and time-dependent pulse dynamics. Finally, an FRQI encoding with Pauli-graph quantum Hadamard edge detection reproduces the classical structural edge score to numerical precision.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, structural diagnostic tool to detect coherent crosstalk in quantum processors by analyzing the residual Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM). It proves that only genuine two-qubit interactions generate a unique, measurable signature in the PTM's cross-weight structure. This signature is then read out using a quantum-native Pauli-graph measurement, providing a robust method to distinguish hardware crosstalk from simple calibration drift.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical challenge of distinguishing between malicious coherent crosstalk (nonlocal interactions) and benign calibration drift (local noise) in multi-tenant quantum processors, especially when both result in the same average gate infidelity.
main_result: A structural verification framework based on the residual Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM) and Pauli-graph Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) was developed, proving that only true two-qubit interactions generate a detectable, non-zero cross-weight signature.
method: The authors use a structural diagnostic based on the signed antisymmetric coupling within the PTM, which is shown to be an isometry for two-qubit interactions. This signature is then read out quantum-natively using an FRQI encoding and Pauli-graph QHED.
model_or_system: The work applies to multi-tenant quantum processors, modeled using Pauli operators and characterized by the Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM). The analysis focuses on distinguishing local, unital noise channels from coherent, non-local two-qubit interaction channels.
key_observables: The primary observable is the signed cross-weight vector $\mathbf{x}$ derived from the residual PTM, and the secondary, quantum-native readout is the Pauli-graph Edge Score $	ext{edge}(S)$.
important_parameters: Detection threshold $\lambda_{\min} \approx 0.13$ (for 16,384 settings), scaling $\propto M^{-1/2}$, and the first-order dependence on interaction strength $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the ability to perform randomized-Pauli measurements and relies on the structural property that local errors yield zero cross-weight mass, while two-qubit interactions do not.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the detection pipeline from shared datasets to the residual PTM, the use of the cross-weight signature, and the final quantum-native readout via Pauli-graph QHED, confirming the detection limit scaling.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the ambiguity between crosstalk and drift using average fidelity, introduces the PTM framework to define a structural signature ($\mathbf{x}$), proves mathematically that this signature separates local from nonlocal errors, and finally implements a quantum-native readout using FRQI and QHED.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, structural diagnostic tool for quantum hardware characterization that moves beyond simple scalar fidelity metrics, which is crucial for scaling quantum computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the framework. One shared randomized-Pauli dataset yields the residual PTM and the signed cross-weight vector x, which is exactly zero for product local unital errors (Proposition 1) and first order in any two-qubit Pauli generator (Proposition 2). The calibrated direction-resolved test on x carries the security decision within the small-rotation scope; the full-block norm b12 is invariant under local rotations (Proposition 3), and the FRQI and Pauli-graph QHED branch is a quantum-native readout of the feature’s structural pattern.
